Use when starting work on this repository, adding a slice or a business question, deciding which layer a change belongs in, or when a change seems to need two layers at once.

- dar: Work on the DAR layer — the generated Unified Star Schema, dab/uss.yaml, and the SQL under dar/uss. Use when adding an event or a measure, changing the bridge's column contract, debugging a total that is wrong or multiplied, or when generated SQL and the model have drifted.
- das: Work on the DAS layer — data contracts, the dlt landing zone, and the raw and staged views. Use when adding or changing a source, editing das/contracts/*.yaml, touching src/adss/{contract,das,landing,source}.py, re-recording fixtures, or debugging why a column is missing, mistyped, or duplicated in das__staged.
- destination: Work on the marimo destination — the page that presents a question and its answer, and the screenshots a slice is accepted on. Use when adding a page for a new question, changing a chart, or when a screenshot is blank, truncated or fails to render.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.

- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.

# Session logs

This branch carries the raw logs of the Claude Code session that built this repository.

It is an orphan branch, deliberately. It shares no commit history with `main` or with any
of the slice branches, so these 25 MB of transcripts never appear in a code diff and never
get dragged into a slice's pull request. Nothing here is part of the codebase. Nothing here
is imported, executed, or referenced by the code on the other branches.

## What the session was

A build of an Analytical Data Storage System (ADSS) as described by the posts on
blog.daana.dev: the three layers (DAS, data according to system; DAB, data according to
business; DAR, data according to requirements) over one DuckDB file, with a marimo page as
the destination that presents a business question and its answer.

It was run under the user's own `grill-to-build` skill, which sets the shape of the work:

- interview to exhaustion, then a plan, then the user confirms it;
- one workflow per vertical slice, thin end to end, widened one slice at a time;
- spikes for what cannot be answered by reading, time-boxed, thrown away, never landed;
- a MADR at each decision, written at the decision;
- red and green in a single conventional commit;
- code review and security review before the user sees the work.

The session opened at 14:50 UTC on 2026-09-07 and this snapshot was taken at 22:33 UTC the
same day. In that time it read the blog, exercised daana-cli end to end, ran four spikes,
scaffolded the repository, and built slice 1 (orders per month and ship country) through to
a screenshotted marimo page. Sixteen commits. Slice 2 (freight per customer country and
quarter) was in progress when the snapshot was taken.

## Why the logs are here

To improve the `grill-to-build` skill.

They are the record of where the process worked and where it did not — not a tutorial and
not a curated highlight reel. The interesting material is mostly in the places where the
skill's instructions and the agent's actual behaviour came apart. There is a section on the
ones already known at the bottom of this file.

## What is here

```
README.md                     this file
session/
  transcript.jsonl            the main session transcript (1,965 events, 6.9 MB)
  subagents/                  one transcript per subagent
    agent-<id>.jsonl            transcript
    agent-<id>.meta.json        agent type, description, spawn depth
    workflows/<run-id>/         subagents grouped by the workflow run that spawned them
      agent-<id>.jsonl
      agent-<id>.meta.json
      journal.jsonl             the workflow's own ledger: step started, step result
  workflows/
    wf_<run-id>.json          run record for a completed workflow
    scripts/<name>-<run-id>.js  the generated workflow script that drove the run
  tool-results/
    <id>.txt                  tool results too large to keep inline in a transcript
```

The main transcript is the spine: the interview, the plan, the user's messages, the
orchestration, and every one of the sixteen commits, which were all issued from the main
session rather than from a subagent. The subagents did the reading, the spikes, the framing of
each slice and the verification, and there is roughly three times as much tool work in their
transcripts as in the main one, so that is where the reasoning behind a given change usually
is.

Six workflow runs, in the order they happened:

| run id            | script name                | what it did                                          |
| ----------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `wf_44ca6cb0-758` | `read-daana-blog`          | one agent per remaining blog post, then a synthesis   |
| `wf_91ac952a-fb2` | `adss-spikes`              | four time-boxed spikes, thrown away after            |
| `wf_ad360891-255` | `slice-01-frame`           | framed and built slice 1                              |
| `wf_8c7d50e0-55b` | `slice-01-verify`          | four verification lenses over slice 1                 |
| `wf_98e86dff-34e` | `slice-01-security-review` | the security review, run late (see below)             |
| `wf_50e62224-d2b` | `slice-02-frame`           | framed slice 2                                        |

Four of the six have a `wf_<run-id>.json` run record. The last two do not: they were still
running when the snapshot was taken, and the record is written when a run finishes.

## Reading a `.jsonl` transcript

One JSON object per line, each one an event in the conversation. Line order is chronological.
The fields that matter most are `type` (`user`, `assistant`, `attachment`, `queue-operation`,
`system`, and a few bookkeeping kinds), `timestamp`, and `message.content`, which is an array
of content blocks — `text`, `tool_use`, `tool_result`. A `user` line that carries a
`toolUseResult` field is a tool result being fed back to the model, not a person talking.

Two things a reader usually wants first.

**Everything the user typed.** Not the `user` lines — in this session those are mostly tool
results. What a person actually typed is recorded as a queue operation:

```sh
jq -r 'select(.type == "queue-operation" and .operation == "enqueue")
       | select((.content | type) == "string")
       | select(.content | startswith("<task-notification>") | not)
       | "\(.timestamp)\n\(.content)\n"' session/transcript.jsonl
```

That returns five messages, which is all the free text the user sent in seven and a half
hours. The rest of the user's input came through structured prompts, and it is worth reading
too — the whole interview lives in the results of `AskUserQuestion` calls, as a map from the
question asked to the option chosen:

```sh
jq -r 'select((.toolUseResult | type) == "object" and .toolUseResult.answers != null)
       | .toolUseResult.answers | to_entries[] | "Q: \(.key)\nA: \(.value)\n"' \
   session/transcript.jsonl
```

The plan and its approval are in the `ExitPlanMode` calls and their results, in the same file.

**Every commit made.** Commits were issued as `git -c user.name=... commit -q -F - <<'MSG'`,
so the literal string `git commit` will not find them, and most were made by subagents rather
than the main session. Search all transcripts at once:

```sh
find session -name '*.jsonl' -exec jq -r '
  select(.type == "assistant") | .message.content[]?
  | select(.type == "tool_use" and .name == "Bash")
  | .input.command | select(test("git .*commit"))' {} + \
  | grep -E "^(feat|fix|docs|chore)\("
```

That returns the sixteen conventional-commit subject lines in the order they were written.
Drop the `grep` to see the full commands and the commit bodies.

These files were copied while the session was still running. The tail of every transcript is
whatever had been written at 22:33 UTC on 2026-09-07, and the session continued afterwards.
The last events in `session/transcript.jsonl` are the ones that produced this branch. Nothing
here is a complete record of the session's end, and the two unfinished workflow runs have no
run record for the reason given above.

One file from `tool-results/` was left out: `bs5ovt1mz.txt`, a spilled tool result that was
still being written at the moment of the snapshot and had reached exactly 64 MiB, the cap at
which such a result is truncated. It began as a fixture manifest and ran on into the raw bytes
of a compiled binary. It is not readable text, it is not greppable, and at 64 MiB it was larger
than everything else on this branch put together. Every other file in those four directories is
here, uncompressed and unmodified.

## Known process failures

The point of the branch. These are the ones already identified, all of them checkable against
the commits on the slice branches and against the transcripts here.

**Five architecture decision records were batched into one commit.** Commit `e81a9af`,
`docs(adr): decide the five records slice 1 rests on`, adds `docs/adr/0001` through `0005` in a
single commit. The skill says a MADR is written at the decision and never batched. The decisions
were taken at different moments during the framing of slice 1 and written up together
afterwards, which is exactly what the rule exists to prevent. They did at least land before the
code they justify — the first feature commit is six minutes later — so the sequencing survived
and only the granularity was lost. The record now shows five decisions arriving simultaneously,
which is not what happened, and the reasoning in each was reconstructed rather than captured.

**The security review was not run when the skill requires it.** The skill puts code review and
security review before the user sees the work. The code review did run in place, and it found a
real bug: commit `3a6ab5b`, `fix(repo): act on the code review, which found a bug that only
bites elsewhere`. The security review did not. Its workflow script,
`session/workflows/scripts/slice-01-security-review-wf_98e86dff-34e.js`, was not written until
22:23 — after slice 1 had been presented to the user, after the last slice-1 commits at 22:15
and 22:17, and a minute after the slice 2 framing workflow had already been authored. It was
started retroactively, as a thing remembered rather than a gate passed.

**The first slice's build was not idempotent, and no review caught it.** `adss build` worked on
a clean checkout and failed on the second run. It surfaced only when slice 2 reran it, and was
fixed in commit `058faa6`, `fix(dab): let the build be run twice, which is the only way it gets
run`. Neither the slice-01 verification workflow (`wf_8c7d50e0-55b`, four lenses over the slice)
nor the code review noticed. This is the most useful of the three, because it is a gap in what
the reviews look for rather than a step that was skipped: they established that the build worked,
not that it could be repeated, and running a build twice is the normal case, not the edge case.

For balance, the process did catch things on its own. The verification workflow found two
problems worth fixing (`3d2fa7e`) and the code review found one (`3a6ab5b`). The failures above
are the places where it did not.

=============== f363004 ===============
fix(repo): make the slice's own assertions capable of failing, and its records true

The verification's recurring theme was not wrong code. It was tests and records that could not
have noticed if the code were wrong.

Three mutations to the version CTE -- the piece of SQL that picks which version of an entity an
event is measured on -- left the whole suite green: row_number to rank, DESC to ASC, and adding
the timestamp to the partition, which makes every retained version a bridge row. The three
assertions guarding it were whole-file substrings, every one of which the INHERIT CTE also
satisfies, so they were about a different window than the one they named. And none of it is
visible in the warehouse, because every entity has exactly one version today. That is the
failure mode ADR 0006 warned about in as many words.

Measure ownership was pinned the same way, and slice 3 is the first slice where it matters,
because ORDER now owns four measures across two stages. Deciding ownership by entity rather
than by event emitted a column the branch's own CTE does not have -- SQL that cannot bind --
and the suite stayed green, because the NULL casts the test looked for were still emitted by
some other branch. Rotating the values within a branch while leaving the aliases in contract
order put a count into a sum column, also green. Both are now asserted as value-to-alias pairs,
per branch, per measure.

Two ADR Confirmation sections named tests that could not fail for the reason given. One claimed
the same measure id on two different entities is still accepted; no fixture contained that case,
so keying the refusal on the id alone -- exactly what the record says it must not do -- left the
suite green. The other claimed definitions() returns one entry per measure, while comparing the
declarations with themselves. Both cases exist now, and both mutations are caught. That is left
in the record rather than tidied away: a Confirmation is only as good as what its test
constructs.

The delivered screenshot for slice 1 changed in this slice with no change to its answer. The
heatmap ordered countries by a sort with ties, which is not stable, so the picture a slice was
accepted on moved between runs from identical data -- and a reviewer diffing the PNG could not
tell a re-sorted tie from a new number. Ties break by name now, and three consecutive renders
produce the same bytes.

Also: the new exactness check had no test that could fail, which is the pattern slice 2
established one commit earlier and this one departed from; its predicate is now a named function
with its own tests. The page indexed a third question unconditionally and divided by a count
read from the data, either of which would fail every question's render rather than one. It
stated "twenty-one orders" as prose on the artefact the slice is accepted on; that number is
computed now, like every other number on the page.

And the records. M5 permitted "a CASE over columns of that row" while M5a forbade "a CASE on
values" -- but every CASE is both, so the pair decided nothing and handed back the argument M5a
exists to close; a CASE is always a choice, so it moves to the forbidden side. ADR 0002's
Confirmation still described the with_rel check that slice 2 replaced. ADR 0007's named a test
in the wrong file and described the guarantee as being about types when it is about values.
ADR 0008 now corrects the sentence of ADR 0002 its own mismatch makes false: with two events on
one entity, a measure is non-null only on the owning EVENT, which _stage does not name. The
question's front matter said sum beside a count measure and named one of the two it returns.
And a test asserted over a source column name, which two hard rules forbid and its neighbours
already avoided.

=============== 26d8af3 ===============
fix(dab): stop the M5 fix from excusing the one thing M5 exists to stop

The verification refused this slice, and on the sharpest possible grounds: the fix I made for
M5's false refusal opened a real hole in the same rule.

Blanking `extract(DAY FROM ...)` was right; blanking it by discarding the whole argument list
was not. A subquery hidden inside one of those calls became invisible to the checker -- so a
reach into another table, which M5 names explicitly and which is the mapping-level enforcement
of the flow rule, was accepted where it had been refused an hour earlier. The scan also counted
raw parentheses, so a bracket inside a string literal unbalanced it and silently discarded
everything after the call: a checker that reads half of what it is given and reports nothing.

Taking simply the next FROM instead is no better, and I only found that by attacking my own
replacement: in `trim(a) FROM elsewhere` the next FROM is the reach. So the scan now finds the
first FROM at the call's own bracket depth, gives up at the bracket that closes the call, and
steps over single-quoted text.

Every clause of that sentence is now pinned by a case that fails without it, which took three
rounds to get right and is the part worth recording. The first cases I wrote did not
discriminate: the literal-skipping and the word-boundary clauses were both exercised only by
expressions where the awkward text came AFTER the keyword, where neither clause matters. It
takes a literal bracket or a "from"-prefixed identifier standing BEFORE the keyword to tell a
correct scan from a broken one. Six mutations, all red now, including the two depth guards
removed together -- each masks the other, so only the pair can be pinned.

Two smaller things from the same review. `coalesce(a, b)` sat in a list headed "are permitted"
while ADR 0007 names a coalesce as the thing the rule does not permit; that is the sentence a
future reader would have cited. And an assertion checking that a refusal names the stray keys
looked for the letter "b", which the refusal message contains in the words "block style"
regardless -- so half the conjunction could never fail.

fix(questions): decide the aggregate refusal on the column, not on the name in front of it

One hole is left and is measured rather than assumed: a column aliased to a `_measure__` name
inside a subquery still gets through. Closing it means resolving aliases rather than reading

instead of leaving it to be found -- and corrects what it said before, which was that the rule
was over-strict at the edge rather than porous there. It was porous.

The walk is a stack rather than recursion. The engine accepts a thousand nested calls, which is
twice what CPython will follow, so seven hundred of them used to come out of the checker as an
unhandled RecursionError -- a refusal nobody can read, on input nobody writes, which is a bad
trade for four lines.

stopping the walk at the top level.

=============== 46668a9 ===============
fix(dar): three defects the verification found, each one a check that could not see it

**A ranking window is not an aggregate.** `row_number`, `rank`, `ntile` and `lag` are all in
duckdb_functions()'s aggregate list, so reading that list alone refused "rank the months" -- an
ordinary shape for an answer -- and told its author to look for a fan-out that is not there. The
engine types the node `WINDOW_ROW_NUMBER` rather than `WINDOW_AGGREGATE`, so the engine settles
it, which is the same reason the function list came from the engine in the first place. Seven
mutations of the refusal now, all caught, including refusing a ranking window again.

**An inherited date could come from a version that blanked it.** The as-of join took the latest
parent version at or before the child's observation, dated or not -- so a source that clears a
date on a correction, which is an ordinary shape in a full change log, gives the child a null
date, and ADR 0009's own rule then removes its row. A whole grain leaves the bridge while the
parent's own event stays dated, and nothing says so.

Which is why the third change is a test file rather than a fix. Every existing test of this
mechanism reads the generated SQL for a shape; none executes it, and both defects above survive
every one of them. `tests/test_inherited_date_sql.py` builds a warehouse where the parent has
more than one version -- which the real one never does, so the real one could not have shown
this -- and asserts the child gets the version in force at its own observation, that a blanked
date is not that version, and that a parent with no dated version at all still yields no row.

**The page indexed row 0 of a filtered frame.** Every month but the last is "whole", so an
answer of one month filters to nothing and the render dies rather than showing the emptiness,
which is the actual news. Guarded, and the sentence it fed is now conditional. The screenshot is
byte-identical.

docs(adr): give one ingest one clock, because two of them silently emptied a stage

Slice 4 is the first slice to read one entity's history as of another entity's observation, and
it found that "the observation" was not one time: a pipeline per contract, landed in sorted
order, so order_details is always stamped a fraction of a second before orders. No ORDER version
precedes any ORDER_LINE row, the inherited date resolves to null for all 2,155 of them, and ADR
0009's own rule removes every one from the bridge.

A clean clone therefore builds an empty stage and q04 returns nothing against the source's 23
rows. It was green here because this tree's gitignored lake had twelve older orders loads, one
of whose versions survives in the history view and carries the same date any newer one would. A
lake that accumulates across runs is a machine for turning a broken build green.

The record says plainly that the fix belongs in DAS and not in the join. Landing in dependency
order would make the layer that fetches data consult the layer whose purpose is not to know
where data came from; falling back to the parent's earliest version changes what "as of" means
and fixes one query rather than the fact.

=============== 8f46de9 ===============
fix(dab): refuse an id this system cannot spell, because it spells them into three places

An id becomes a quoted SQL identifier, a string literal inside a generated check, and the stem
of a file under checks/. A security review found both ways that matters.

An event id of `O' AND 1 = 0 --` closes the literal a measure check puts it in and comments out
the rest, so the check emits, formats, lints and runs -- and reports nothing wrong for ever.
That is the failure this repository cares most about: an assertion that cannot fail. An entity
id of `../../../tmp/PWNED` makes `adss dar generate` write its check outside checks/ entirely.

Neither is an escalation and the record should not pretend otherwise. Whoever can edit these
files can already run arbitrary SQL: the engine compiles a mapping's transformation expressions
verbatim into views over the same warehouse, and the formatter is not a validator -- injected
multi-statement SQL passes through it unchanged. These are refused because a name that means
one thing in a file and another in SQL is a bug waiting for an unlucky source, not because a
door is being closed.

One rule, in names.py, applied by the three readers that take an id from a file: the model, the
declarations and the mappings. A letter, then letters, digits and underscores. The repository's
own ids are asserted against it, so the rule is not one nothing obeys.

docs(skills): write down what the second grain taught

The DAR skill's central rule said keys inherit and measures do not, and left it there. It now
carries the measurement -- 2,155 line rows against an order's freight that does not move -- and
the half that is false beside it: the bridge protects the measure column and not the attribute
it was made from, so one join and one sum over the peripheral returns 207,306.10 against a true
64,942.69. A third query-time rule follows, because the first two did not cover it.

Also the inherited date, which is the other thing this slice added and the one whose failure is
invisible: a row whose inherited date does not resolve gets no bridge row, filtered where the
date was resolved rather than where the event's own date is, because the alternative arrives
dated null and is dropped by the calendar's inner join -- which looks exactly like the rule
working.

The destination skill gains two rules learned by getting them wrong. A page invents no fact: no
currency symbol where the model records no currency. And a series has to stop somewhere, so the
period it stops inside is short rather than small -- fade it, caption it, and derive which one
it is from the answer rather than from a date the page was told.

The ADSS skill gains the one that has now cost twice: run the mutation before the ADR's
Confirmation claims one. A confirmation naming a test that could not fail for the reason given
is worse than no confirmation, because it stops anybody looking again.

feat(dar): check that an inherited date agrees with the stage that owns it

ADR 0009's Confirmation described this check an hour after the decision landed. It did not
exist -- nothing emitted it and no file was in checks/ -- and a security review found the
sentence. It is the third confirmation here to name a check that could not do what it said,
which is why the rule about running the mutation first now lives in the adss skill. The
sentence is true as of this commit rather than withdrawn.

It compares the two stages rather than re-deriving the date. The parent's own stage gets it
from its version CTE and the child's from its inherit CTE, so resolving the date at a different
instant than the key, or against a different version of the parent, shows up as a disagreement.
A check that computed the expected date the way the generator does would have agreed with a
broken generator, which is the trap the bridge's column contract already carries a note about.

Generated only where the entity the date comes from has an event on that same attribute --
without one there is nothing independent to compare against. 2,155 comparisons on the real
build, and a synthetic bridge in tests/ where it goes red.

What it does not see is written into the record rather than left to be found: a row dropped
because its inherited date did not resolve is absent, and an absent row disagrees with nothing.
Checking that needs a count of the rows a stage should have, and nothing in the model states
one -- a line whose order has no date is legitimately absent, and no check can tell that from a
line the generator lost.

Forty-eight checks pass.
